fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Next comes the food: she has prepared her meat, mixed her wine and set her table. Her house is built and dinner is ready. I've pulled a batch out of the oven with the doorbell already ringing, so a host with the table set gets my respect.

Not quite, friend. Wisdom has sent out her maidservants, and she calls out from the heights of the city (Proverbs 9:3). That's a host who has sent people out and is calling out herself. Waiting quietly inside isn't what the verse shows.
Not quite, friend. She says, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live…” The promise is life, not wandering. Walking in the way of understanding is the opposite of drifting around lost.
That's not what she promises, baker. Her words are, “Leave your folly behind, and you will live…” Wisdom's invitation points toward life. Suffering isn't the word she uses.

Yes, baker. The passage says, “He who corrects a mocker brings shame on himself…” The one who steps up to correct a mocker walks away with shame. Sometimes the kindest move is to save your breath and keep your own apron clean.

That's right, baker. The passage says, “rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” (Proverbs 9:8) The wise man will love the one who rebukes him. Compare that with the mocker, who, the verse says, will hate you. It's a good reminder to be the wise one when a correction comes my way.

It's actually true, friend. The text says, “rebuke a wise man, and he will love you.” The mocker will hate the one who rebukes him, but the wise man will love him. That's the difference between the two of them in this verse.

Study is a fine thing, friend, but that's not what this verse names. It says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom…” That's where the verse says wisdom begins. Starting at the right place matters more than how long you've been going.

No battles in this promise, baker. The verse says, “For through wisdom your days will be multiplied, and years will be added to your life.” Days multiplied, years added, and not a single sword gets mentioned. I'll take the years and skip the fights.
Rest is a nice idea, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says, “but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.” Scoff is the word that fits the second blank.

Waiting doesn't fit here, baker. The verse says, “If you are wise, you are wise to your own advantage; but if you scoff, you alone will bear the consequences.” Wait isn't in the verse. The words that fit are wise and scoff.
Yes, baker. Folly says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and Wisdom said those same words in Proverbs 9:4. The opening words are an exact match. I think that's worth slowing down for.
Softer isn't something the verse says, baker. Folly says, “Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!” and Wisdom used those same words in Proverbs 9:4. The opening line is an exact match.
No market in her pitch, friend. Folly says, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Her line about bread is that bread eaten in secret is tasty. Price never comes up.

Folly doesn't say that, baker. Her words are, “Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is tasty!” Her line is about bread eaten in secret, not bread shared with friends. A bakery full of friends sounds better to me.

A royal feast isn't in the verse, friend. The passage says the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (Proverbs 9:18). It's a heavy verse. Her pitch is about sweet water and tasty bread, and the truth is something else.

Treasure isn't what the passage names, baker. It says the dead are there, and that her guests are in the depths of Sheol (Proverbs 9:18). It's a heavy line. The pitch sounds tasty, but the verse tells what's really there.

Not quite, friend. The passage says, “But they do not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol.” They don't know. That's the trouble with her pitch, because the people walking in don't know what's there.
